Was there a ledger to square: Britain’s rule in Nigeria by Lawson Akhigbe

The late Sam Mbakwe, first civilian governor of Imo State and a man whose impatience with mediocrity remains legendary, once declared that he would gladly invite the British back to rule Nigeria for another fifty years. I have been wondering for a while what to write about standardized testing, which used to be so important in my life—there was a small chance all along that I might have fallen into the right-wing eugenicist trap of equating high #test scores to "objective proof" of intellectual and genetic superiority. It is too easy to see why this has happened: U.S. #education is a wasteland of destructive policies and censored textbooks and the primary goal of school is to act like a half-way house between childhood and either FORCED labor (as a prisoner) or ostensibly voluntary labor in the U.S. #economy.

The standardized tests are best regarded as roughly equivalent to civil service exams or placement exams in the Army or similar: they're for sorting and screening. The few deemed useful and promising to the ruling class get plucked out of this system, sifted to the top all along the way; everyone else gets to endure year after year of being placed in one category or another.

It's a massive business which has given shady profit-seeking corporations such as the "College Board" (cute marketing trick, the bland bureaucratic name) a ridiculous degree of power over education and U.S. social status, a position which has been reinforced by the mystical arm of psychometry: Charles Murray and friends, who sift through SAT and GRE scores as if they were the entrails of a freshly slaughtered goat in the hands of the Empress Livia Drusilla restlessly seeking any information as to the direction of the Roman state. It was deadly serious business to her, to read the auspices correctly; thus have eugenicists come to place extreme faith in multiple-choice tests.

Racists on Twitter blither about their "great predictive power" because it's practically a circular argument: in a society which forces people to be sorted according to test results, the results correlate greatly with social standing and "intelligence"! They see their own imposed bias and smile, and if you point out the nature of the bias they block you without acknowledging the comment.

But in this fanatical determination to exalt standardized tests there's a hint of something else: racists mire themselves in racism as an alternative to accepting humiliation from some massive fuckup or social quarrel, so these are not happy and successful people generally. Even Charles Murray, still respectable and boasting of his political connections, was once aiming MUCH higher in life. Compared to genuine academic standing, a pile of right-wing "fellowships" from institutions that specialize entirely in warehousing right-wingers who wash out of more respectable professional posts must feel like a mean prize indeed to Dr. Charles Murray (btw #MIT really should claim credit for that old charlatan.)

So if you're a person of meager achievements, what can you take pride in? SAT scores from when you were sixteen, maybe. (I took it once, in 9th grade, so I was 13. I didn't prep for it, I got 800 math and 750 verbal.) It's like deciding that the high point of your life was that one time you were the third-string quarterback for the Podunk Shitkickers in school, or that you were at your peak when you ran for class president. The United States mainstream culture is drowning in such grade-school nostalgia. It's got an ugly side (q.v. American Beauty.)

Even I was somewhat vulnerable. After Amazon dot com chewed me up and I could get no better work than temp clerical stuff, I decided to take a few standardized tests. There was a practical excuse: I was revisiting the idea of graduate school so I needed GRE scores. But I took the MCAT for fun mostly (36 out of 50 and I got torrents of medical school brochures in the mail) mostly because I was hurting and discouraged and I wanted the cheap feeling of approval again. It had once seemed an achievement to get a high AP exam score or whatever. I was willing to pay for it again...and there must surely be people who put way much more adult time and money into grinding out high scores on exams that now are irrelevant to them career-wise, but good for bragging rights and fortifying one's faith in The Bell Curve.

And one more thing: what's to stop racists from paying a little MORE money for the sole purpose of giving "Black" test-takers lower scores? The #SAT people don't know who's actually taking the test. It's all become so computerized that you could probably rig an LLM bot to register for SAT testing. It's so easy to load up the records with faked-up data that only a fool would think that distributions of SAT scores were trustworthy and "objective"... either a fool, or a think-tank darling with a Rolodex of corporate bosses and conservative politicians.

~Chara of Pnictogen

Over 2025-2026, Beijing, Shenzhen, Hangzhou, and Chongqing released a wave of AI industrial policies. Western coverage calls it "catching the AI wave." Lay the policy documents side by side and a different logic emerges: this is a debt resolution play, and AI is the only path that doesn't make anyone eat the loss.

First Principles: Debt Is Borrowed Future Productivity


There are exactly three ways to resolve debt:

  1. The debtor takes the loss (1990s, 30 million SOE workers laid off)
  2. The creditor takes the loss (inflation diluting savings)
  3. Productivity explodes and covers it (a technology revolution)

China tried the first two. Each cost a generation. The third option — AI creating enough new value to cover old debt — is the comparatively gentler one.

What the Red-Header Documents Actually Say

CityDocumentRefDebt angleShenzhenAI Terminal Industry Action Plan深工信〔2025〕42号special funds for strategic industriesHangzhouAI Innovation Hub Implementation杭政函〔2025〕65号¥100B fund, ¥250M compute vouchersChongqing"AI+" Action Planref # not publicly releasedintelligent upgrade of 33,618-manufacturing clustersBeijingAgent-Industry Acceleration Measuresref # not publicly releasedGalaxy Compute Corridor, Token vouchers


The central government set the tone in the 2026 Government Work Report: "resolve debt through development, develop through debt resolution."

Local Financing Platforms: From Debt Vehicles to Tech Shareholders


As of February 2026, 1,028 LGFV entities have formally "left the platform" (public LGFV transition data). Rizhao, Chengdu's Wenjiang district, and Tangshan's Industrial Holdings (¥947M acquisition of a listed company) are all converting from infrastructure debt vehicles into holders of technology assets. Debt resolution and industrial transformation, executed as a single move.

Global AI Governance: Three Approaches


  • EU: strictest — AI Act effective 2024.8.1, fully applicable 2026.8.2, four risk tiers, fines up to €35M or 7% of global turnover (Act text). 45 European firms publicly opposed it for "stifling innovation."
  • US: fragmented — states legislate separately, top five AI labs joined a voluntary evaluation system.

China Extends A Friendly Panda Paw: USA-PRC Alliance?

If I read well between the lines, China asserts that there is a de facto alliance with the USA.

Dozens of top Chinese senior generals were fired in 2025-2026. The Chinese military commission found itself with only two members, and President Xi was one of the two. China not being a democracy, speculation ran rampant about what it all meant.

One theory full of hope was that some of the old fashion generals wanted to attack Taiwan, and Xi did not. Indeed, attacking Taiwan would have been madness: it would have shattered the integration of China in the Global Empire, and probably failed. The war in Ukraine was an excellent warning, of what happens when a tyrant decides to attack the Empire Of Democracy, and Ukraine doesn’t have the insulating sea and very high mountains of Taiwan: Taiwan is an invasion nightmare, long a redoubt for pirates, Ming remnants, and a place which the French failed to occupy, in great part because of the impossible landscape. The EOD, the Empire Of Democracy has excellent attack submarines (US subs sank a lot of the Japanese Navy and merchant fleet in those waters in 1944-45) And the EOD makes 85% of its advanced electronic chips in Taiwan… So the EOD would have defended Taiwan (whereas the EOD has little economically at stake in Ukraine, but for the idea of democracy).

So Xi seems indeed to have gotten rid of his Taiwanophobic generals, indeed, and that’s excellent news. Better invade the Moon than a mountain in the ocean, next to the world’s most busy trading route. The more powerful China gets, the more cooperative Taiwan will be, so peace through a bulldozing economy is the right way to incorporate Taiwan. Here is the text of his discourse at the White House, after removing trivial parts about pandas, students and air travel:

WASHINGTON, Sept. 24 — Chinese President Xi Jinping:

Honorable President Donald J. Trump and Mrs. Melania Trump, Ladies and Gentlemen, Dear Friends,

I’m very glad to pay a state visit to your beautiful country, the United States of America. Thank you, President Trump and Mrs. Trump, for the warm hospitality you have extended to me and my wife. On behalf of the 1.4 billion and more Chinese people, I wish to begin by extending sincere greetings to the American people and warm congratulations on the 250th anniversary of the U.S. independence.

Both China and the United States are great countries, and both the Chinese and American peoples are great peoples. I am visiting the United States at President Trump’s invitation to carry on our friendship, expand cooperation, and promote the well-being of both our peoples.

Facing the changes in our world, in our times, and of historical significance today, China and the United States, as two major countries, shoulder a historic responsibility of advancing human development and progress.

Mr. President, during your visit to China this year, we agreed to build a constructive China-U.S. relationship of strategic stability, and this is widely welcomed by the people of our two countries and the international community. I am ready to work with you to steer the giant ship of China-U.S. relationship on a steady course toward the future.

— We should strengthen communication. China and the United States are different in national conditions, but through candid, in-depth and continued dialogue, our two countries can understand each other better, seek common ground while shelving differences, and build up mutual trust. President Trump and I have respect for each other. We have built personal rapport and stayed in touch. We encourage our government departments, such as those in charge of foreign affairs, economic matters, financial cooperation, law enforcement and people-to-people exchanges, to catch up on strengthening contact, and we support our legislative bodies in increasing exchanges.

— We should cooperate with sincerity. The interests of China and the United States are deeply intertwined, and there is plenty of room for us to work together. China-U.S. cooperation may not solve every problem in the world. But, without our cooperation, it would be hard to solve many of the world’s problems. China keeps its door wide open, welcomes American companies wanting to invest and do business there. We hope Chinese companies are treated fairly here in the United States. Working together, we can lengthen the list of cooperation, and shorten the list of issues. Both China and the United States are leading nations in artificial intelligence. We have both the capability and responsibility to develop and manage AI for good, and ensure that the development of AI is always under human control…

— We should coexist in peace. As I have said many times, China and the United States, as two major countries, stand to gain from cooperation and will both lose in confrontation. We do not need to avoid mentioning competition, but our competition should be a healthy one and should be kept within bounds. It should be a race of catching up with one another, not a wrestle in which one either wins or loses. China and the United States must hold the line of no conflict and no confrontation between us, and we can certainly find the right path for our two great countries to get along on this planet we both call home. Our two militaries should maintain regular dialogue, and improve mechanisms for crisis communication and prevention. The Thucydides Trap can be overcome...Dear Friends,

During the Second World War, Chinese and Americans fought shoulder to shoulder against fascist aggression. Chinese people have never forgotten that part of history, nor have the American people…Dear Friends,

Achieving the great rejuvenation of the Chinese nation and making America great again can go hand in hand. Let us meet the people’s expectation and show our historical initiative. Let us keep advancing the cause of friendship between our two peoples and work together to build a better world!

Thank you.

***

So Xi sounds deep, wise, rational, and caring for humanity in general, just the opposite of nuclear tyrant Putin. What is there not to like? The most advanced innovation is still on the democratic side, though. One may wonder why Europe is not capable to keep up with China and the USA. Simple: Europe is not concentrated upon technical progress as much. Anymore. Basically Europe does not believe as much as it used to, in calculus and engineering.

Correlation is not causation, yes, but clearly the relationship between Chinese GDP growth collapse and trade collapse is clear. A parallel declaration proclaimed the importance of international straits: Iran is blocking, or hindering two, and China needs its oil (which comes from Iran by boat).

It goes without saying that the rest of the world can learn from the Chinese-US tango. What basically China is doing is that, instead of opposing (like the clown of the Kremlin) the world order of 1945, China pretends to have made it bicephalic…

That is why Denmark signed an agreement with the USA on Greenland, with an expanded US military presence, with two new large bases, and restrictions on non NATO investments.

This is all very good, because, in the end, the fate of humanity will be played on the Moon, not between schoolyard bullies beating each other up. Over five months, Trump and Xi met, or planned to meet, four times… Communications, indeed. Meanwhile Europe, as usual, is leaderless, aimless, adrift, and mindless. .

Patrice Ayme

DON’T REPEAT OUR MISTAKE

Botswana’s Diamonds, Africa’s Resources and the Next Development Question

By Joshua Shipepe Hadula

PLNNABLOG_Dont_Repeat_Our_Mistake_Joshua_Shipepe_HadulaDownload

PLNNABLOG | Africa • Resources • Economy • Agriculture • Leadership • Sustainability

“From extraction to transformation.”

1. THE WARNING

Former Botswana President Mokgweetsi Masisi has been associated with a warning to Nigeria and other resource-rich African countries: natural-resource wealth can generate enormous national income, but countries still have to decide what they will build beyond the resource itself.

The underlying economic question is bigger than diamonds.

What happens when the commodity cycle changes?

Botswana provides an important case study because diamonds helped transform the country’s economy, while the country’s present diversification challenge shows the risks of depending heavily on one export sector. The IMF has repeatedly highlighted Botswana’s need to diversify beyond diamonds. (IMF eLibrary)

2. THE DIAMOND THAT CHANGED BOTSWANA

Diamonds became central to Botswana’s post-independence development.

Mining revenues supported infrastructure, public services and macroeconomic stability. The IMF has described Botswana as an unusual example of a resource-rich country that converted mineral wealth into substantial economic development. (IMF)

But success creates its own question:

Can yesterday’s successful economic model remain tomorrow’s successful economic model?

3. THE OTHER SIDE OF THE DIAMOND

The diamond economy has also created concentration.

The IMF reported that diamonds accounted for almost 90% of Botswana’s goods exports over much of the previous decade. When global diamond demand weakened, the country’s economic growth was affected. (IMF eLibrary)

That is the vulnerability behind the diversification debate.

A country can have:

Natural resources + good governance + strong institutions

and still face exposure to:

commodity prices + external demand + finite reserves + technological substitution.

4. THE MARKET HAS CHANGED

The global diamond industry is changing.

The IMF’s 2025 assessment noted weaker natural-diamond demand, competition from lab-grown diamonds and large inventories. It also reported that Botswana’s economy contracted sharply in 2024 as mining output and diamond trading declined. (IMF eLibrary)

This does not mean diamonds have become irrelevant.

It means that a resource-dependent country has to prepare for changing market conditions.

5. MASISI’S OWN MESSAGE: INVEST THE REVENUE

There is an important nuance to the story.

In a 2022 Botswana government report, Masisi said Botswana intended to reinvest diamond proceeds into value addition and economic diversification, so that the benefits of mineral wealth could extend beyond the life of the mines. (Daily News)

That makes the broader lesson more precise:

The issue is not diamonds versus development.

It is:

How does a country turn diamond wealth into a wider productive economy?

6. NIGERIA — A DIFFERENT RESOURCE STORY

Nigeria’s circumstances are different from Botswana’s.

Its resource base includes oil and gas alongside agriculture, manufacturing, services and other minerals.

That difference matters.

The lesson cannot simply be:

“Nigeria will become Botswana.”

Rather, Botswana provides a comparative case study for thinking about resource dependence.

The question for Nigeria and other African economies is:

How much resource revenue becomes productive capacity outside the resource sector?

7. THE RESOURCE-CURSE QUESTION

Academic research gives this debate another dimension.

A study of resource-dependent economies in sub-Saharan Africa from 1999–2019 found that many countries struggled to convert commodity windfalls into sufficiently broad economic diversification. It identifies challenges including Dutch-disease effects, isolated resource sectors and institutional constraints. (ScienceDirect)

But Botswana also demonstrates why the phrase “resource curse” should not be used mechanically.

Botswana achieved substantial development from its mineral wealth.

The more useful question is:

What institutional and economic structures determine how resource wealth is converted into long-term development?

8. FROM MINE TO FACTORY

This is where value addition becomes important.

Instead of exporting only:

ore → diamond → raw commodity

the development ambition becomes:

resource → processing → skills → technology → manufacturing → services → exports.

Botswana’s government has recently emphasized the need to move beyond exporting raw resources and develop manufacturing, agro-processing and local processing capacity. (Government of Botswana)

9. AGRICULTURE IS PART OF THE ANSWER

The photograph supplied for this cover is powerful because it moves the conversation away from the mine.

It places a farmer in a productive field.

That creates a second development equation:

Mineral wealth → investment → agriculture → food security → agro-processing → employment.

The IMF has identified agriculture, manufacturing, tourism and financial services among the areas Botswana could develop alongside mineral resources. (IMF eLibrary)

10. THE FIELD AND THE MINE

The image can therefore be read symbolically.

Behind the farmer: production.

Beyond the farmer: infrastructure.

Under the ground: minerals.

Above the ground: food.

The development challenge is connecting all four.

A mine can generate foreign exchange.

A farm can generate food.

A factory can generate value addition.

A technology company can generate intellectual property.

A financial system can mobilise capital.

The diversified economy connects them.

11. AFRICA’S RESOURCE MAP

Africa possesses enormous reserves of minerals, hydrocarbons, agricultural land and renewable-energy potential.

The strategic question is therefore not simply:

“What does Africa have?”

It is:

“What does Africa manufacture, own, process and export from what it has?”

That distinction separates extraction from industrial development.

12. THE NEW AFRICAN VALUE CHAIN

A modern resource strategy can be visualised as:

RESOURCE

↓

PROCESSING

↓

LOCAL SUPPLIERS

↓

SKILLS

↓

TECHNOLOGY

↓

MANUFACTURING

↓

EXPORTS

↓

TAX REVENUE

↓

EDUCATION + INFRASTRUCTURE

↓

NEW BUSINESSES

This is the transformation from resource economy to productive ecosystem.

13. BOTSWANA’S NEXT CHAPTER

Botswana is already attempting diversification.

The IMF’s 2025 assessment describes efforts involving agriculture, manufacturing, tourism, financial services and other mining opportunities. It also notes the establishment of the Diamonds for Development Fund, intended to support diversification beyond diamond mining. (IMF eLibrary)

In 2026, Botswana government messaging has also highlighted value addition, agro-processing and local processing. (Government of Botswana)

So the story is not simply “Botswana failed.”

It is more accurately:

Botswana succeeded with diamonds—and now has to build the next economic model.

14. THE AFRICAN POLICY QUESTION

For Namibia, Botswana, Nigeria, Angola, Zambia, Zimbabwe, the DRC and other resource-rich economies, five questions deserve attention:

1. OWNERSHIP

Who owns the resource?

2. REVENUE

How much national revenue does it generate?

3. VALUE ADDITION

Where is processing taking place?

4. SKILLS

Who acquires the technical knowledge?

5. DIVERSIFICATION

What survives when commodity prices fall?

15. THE GENERATIONAL TEST

The ultimate measure of resource wealth is not the size of the mine.

It is what remains after the mine’s best years.

Does the country have:

  • engineers?
  • farmers?
  • manufacturers?
  • entrepreneurs?
  • universities?
  • technology companies?
  • export industries?
  • strong infrastructure?
  • financial institutions?
  • local intellectual property?

If the answer is yes, the resource has helped build an economy.

16. THE PLNNABLOG CONCLUSION

DON’T REPEAT THE MISTAKE — BUT UNDERSTAND THE LESSON

The strongest interpretation of the Botswana experience is not that diamonds were a mistake.

They were an enormous source of national development.

The lesson is that a successful commodity can become a vulnerability if diversification does not keep pace with structural changes in the global economy. That concern is particularly relevant today as Botswana faces weaker diamond demand, changing consumer markets and competition from lab-grown diamonds. (IMF eLibrary)

The next African development model therefore needs to connect:

MINERALS

+

AGRICULTURE

+

MANUFACTURING

+

TECHNOLOGY

+

FINANCE

+

HUMAN CAPITAL

=

A MORE DIVERSIFIED ECONOMY

DANGOTE & THE POWER OF NON-STATE ENTITIES

How private industrial giants shape Africa’s supply chains, energy security and economic sovereignty

A private-sector perspective on Dangote’s refinery, African industrialisation and the future of Namibia–Africa economic cooperation.

By Joshua Shipepe Hadula PLNNABLOG | Policy, Law & National News Analysis

THE BIG IDEA

Africa’s economic independence is influenced not only by governments, but also by private entities that control essential infrastructure, production, logistics and distribution.

Dangote’s refinery in Nigeria provides a case study of how African-owned industrial infrastructure can reshape regional trade while raising questions about market concentration, consumer protection and the balance between private commercial power and public interests.

The opportunity for Namibia and other African economies is to understand how to benefit from large industrial gateways while maintaining competition, supply alternatives and transparent regulation.

FEATURE ARTICLE • SEPTEMBER 2026

1. When a private company becomes an African economic gateway

Africa’s economic life is increasingly shaped by large companies that operate beyond the traditional boundaries of the state. These organisations invest in refineries, ports, railways, telecommunications, energy, food production and financial infrastructure.

Unlike a government ministry, a private industrial group makes investment and operational decisions through its corporate structure. Yet when its infrastructure becomes central to national supply chains, those decisions can affect consumers, manufacturers, transport operators and neighbouring countries.

Dangote’s refinery in Nigeria illustrates this relationship between private capital and public economic interests.

6

The question is not simply whether a private company can build a refinery. It is whether an entire region can develop industrial capacity without becoming excessively dependent on a single commercial gateway.

The phrase “holding Africa on the neck” is used in this article as a metaphor for structural dependence, rather than as an allegation that Dangote or any other company controls Africa.

2. Dangote’s refinery: an industrial turning point

The Dangote Petroleum Refinery is located in the Lekki Free Zone near Lagos, Nigeria. It began operations in January 2024.

6

The facility’s crude-processing capacity reached 700,000 barrels per day following maintenance and expansion work completed in February 2026, according to the U.S. Energy Information Administration.

U.S. Energy Information Administration (EIA)

The industrial gateway in numbers

700,000

Barrels per day of crude-processing capacity, reported in August 2026

650,000

Barrels per day of original nameplate capacity

Source: U.S. Energy Information Administration, 24 August 2026.

U.S. Energy Information Administration (EIA)

The importance of the refinery extends beyond Nigeria’s domestic petrol market. It produces petroleum products for regional and international markets and forms part of a broader industrial system involving petrochemicals, storage, marine transport and distribution.

According to the EIA, Nigeria’s seaborne petroleum-product exports averaged 561,000 barrels per day in the second quarter of 2026, compared with an annual average of 79,000 barrels per day in 2023. The agency linked the growth primarily to the refinery’s start-up and subsequent expansion.

U.S. Energy Information Administration (EIA)

This demonstrates how one industrial project can alter the direction of trade: a country that previously imported significant quantities of refined products can become a supplier to other markets.

3. Gateway or gatekeeper? Understanding non-state economic power

A non-state entity is an organisation that is not itself a government. Examples include private industrial conglomerates, international commodity traders, logistics operators, financial institutions and infrastructure companies.

Their influence can grow when they own or operate assets that are difficult to replace.

6

A company can be commercially successful while governments still face difficult public-policy questions.

For example, if several countries rely on one refinery for a large share of their fuel imports, they need to understand the consequences of maintenance shutdowns, transport disruptions, contract changes and price movements.

These are questions of market structure and supply resilience. They do not, by themselves, establish that a company has acted unlawfully or abused its position.

4. From Nigeria to the wider African market

Dangote’s industrial ambitions are no longer limited to West Africa.

In July 2026, Reuters reported that Dangote Group planned to develop a proposed 700,000-barrel-per-day refinery in Lamu, Kenya, with financing expected to include internal cash, bonds and an initial public offering. The project was described as a proposed development, not an operating refinery.

Reuters

6

If implemented, a refinery in East Africa would have implications for fuel supply routes, regional trade and infrastructure planning.

The broader industrial question is how African countries can develop a connected energy market while retaining independent supply options and the ability to negotiate contracts that reflect their own economic conditions.

This is particularly relevant to countries that import most of their refined petroleum products.

5. The limits of industrial self-sufficiency

A refinery located on African soil does not automatically guarantee affordable fuel.

On 21 September 2026, Reuters reported that Nigerian petrol prices had risen amid higher international crude prices, even as the Dangote refinery operated at full capacity. The report attributed the price pressure in part to rising global crude costs.

Reuters

5

This distinction matters because energy security has several separate components:

  • Physical availability of fuel.
  • Affordability for households and businesses.
  • Reliability of transportation and distribution.
  • Access to alternative suppliers.
  • Exposure to exchange rates and international crude prices.

Domestic refining can reduce reliance on imported finished products, but crude oil itself may still be purchased at internationally influenced prices. Transport, taxation, financing and distribution also affect the final price.

The policy question is therefore not only whether Africa can refine its own petroleum, but how countries can translate industrial production into dependable and affordable access.

6. What Namibia can learn from the Dangote model

Namibia has its own energy, port, petroleum-import and natural-resource considerations. Nigeria’s experience should be treated as a case study rather than a ready-made blueprint.

7

For Namibia, a practical assessment of regional industrial partnerships could focus on the following:

A Namibia–Africa industrial cooperation framework

Port and logistics infrastructure

Examine how port capacity, storage, shipping routes and inland transport affect delivered petroleum prices and supply reliability.

Competition and market regulation

Assess supplier concentration, licensing requirements, pricing transparency and the availability of alternative suppliers.

Regional commercial agreements

Explore transparent purchasing arrangements and supply contracts that account for product quality, freight, insurance, delivery reliability and price-review terms.

Local skills and industrial participation

Consider technical training, local services, engineering capability and opportunities for Namibian businesses to participate in industrial supply chains.

The objective would be to assess commercial opportunities and risks using Namibia’s own energy demand, infrastructure, laws and economic priorities.

7. A public-interest framework for engaging large private entities

Large industrial companies can bring investment, technology, jobs and productive infrastructure. Public institutions, meanwhile, remain responsible for establishing rules that protect competition, consumers and the environment.

The following measures offer a framework for discussion.

The key distinction is between the ability of a company to operate at continental scale and the responsibility of governments to ensure that markets remain accountable to the public.

Private investment and public oversight are not mutually exclusive. They can operate together through clear contracts, effective regulation, independent monitoring and transparent reporting.

Conclusion: Africa needs gateways—and choices

Dangote’s refinery demonstrates how African private capital can build infrastructure with regional and international significance. It also raises an important question for the continent: how can Africa expand its industrial capacity without creating new forms of excessive dependence?

The answer involves more than building factories. It requires competitive markets, infrastructure alternatives, capable regulators, skilled workers, transparent commercial arrangements and regional cooperation.

For Namibia, the subject is relevant to the wider conversation about energy security, industrial development, logistics and the future role of African enterprises in regional supply chains.

A gateway can connect economies, create industrial opportunities and strengthen trade. Its long-term public value also depends on whether countries retain meaningful choices, reliable alternatives and the capacity to negotiate in the public interest.

The African industrial future is not simply about who owns the largest refinery. It is about how industrial power, public institutions and economic opportunity work together across the continent.

▪️Uncertain status: Iraq—rumors have circulated regarding the suspension of Iran-Iraq flights starting Tuesday, but neither Iran nor the Iraqi Civil Aviation Authority has confirmed this.

✍Important note:
